planting.note: Root 3-4 inch stem tip cuttings in spring and grow on in a hanging basket or shallow pot of fast-draining mix.

directions: Root 3-4 inch stem tip cuttings in spring, then grow in a hanging basket with bright, indirect light and consistently moist but well-drained soil. The thick, glossy leaves store water like a succulent, so this gesneriad tolerates brief dry spells better than most of its relatives, though it blooms best with regular fertilizing through the growing season. Its curved, inflated orange flowers genuinely resemble tiny goldfish poking out of the foliage, a distinctive trait shared across the Nematanthus clan but especially pronounced here. Pinch growing tips after flowering to keep the trailing stems bushy rather than leggy.

planting.note: Plant the small scaly rhizomes just under the soil surface in spring in a loose, peaty mix and keep warm until growth appears.

directions: Plant the small scaly rhizomes just under the surface of a loose, peaty mix in spring and keep the pot warm and evenly moist until velvety, maroon-tinted leaves emerge. Grow in bright shade with high humidity, since the fuzzy foliage scorches in direct sun or dry air. Nodding cinnabar-red tubular flowers rise above the foliage in late summer, giving the plant the 'temple bells' name it shares with hybrid Smithiantha. After bloom the top growth dies back naturally; withhold water and store the dormant rhizomes cool and dry until repotting the following spring.

planting.note: Divide scaly rhizomes in spring and set them shallowly in a humus-rich, well-drained mix.

directions: Divide the scaly underground rhizomes in spring and set them shallowly in a humus-rich, well-drained mix, then keep the soil evenly moist through the growing season. Give the plant bright, indirect light and some humidity, since the soft, hairy leaves can scorch under direct sun. The tubular, speckled pink-and-white flowers nod from arching stems and are noticeably longer and more foxglove-like than the showier hybrid Kohlerias commonly sold as houseplants. Cut stems back hard after flowering to encourage fresh rhizome growth and a second flush of bloom.

planting.note: Set rooted divisions or stem cuttings into moist, humus-rich soil in a shaded spot after frost danger passes.

directions: Set rooted divisions or stem cuttings into moist, humus-rich soil in a shaded spot in spring, since this South African forest-floor relative of Tradescantia spreads readily from creeping, somewhat succulent stems. It tolerates deeper shade than most Commelinaceae groundcovers and forms a loose, spreading mat useful under trees or along a shaded border. Small three-petaled blue flowers open briefly in the morning along the stem tips through summer, followed by quick regrowth if the stems are cut back. Keep the soil consistently moist, since the fleshy stems wilt quickly in dry conditions.

planting.note: Grow in a shallow pot or terrarium with a loose, well-drained mix and high humidity.

directions: Grow this miniature gesneriad in a shallow pot or terrarium with a loose, well-drained mix, high humidity, and shaded, indirect light, since the small rosette-forming leaves are intolerant of dry air and direct sun. The leaves are distinctively patterned with silvery spots on a dark green background, and established clumps slowly spread via tiny underground tubers that can be divided to start new pots. Thin, wiry flower stalks rise well above the foliage bearing small fringed pink and white blooms, an unusual proportion for such a tiny plant. Keep it out of cold drafts, since it is strictly a warm terrarium or greenhouse subject outside the tropics.

planting.note: Divide fleshy rhizomes in spring and plant in a rich, consistently moist mix in a warm, shaded spot.

directions: Divide the fleshy rhizomes in spring and plant in a rich, consistently moist mix, since this gesneriad grows naturally along Central American streambanks and does not tolerate drying out between waterings. Give it bright shade and warmth; the glossy, coppery-green leaves and upright stems form a tidy, bushy clump rather than trailing like related Nematanthus and Columnea species. Small yellow tubular flowers emerge from inflated red calyces held close to the stem, a two-toned effect distinct from the plain yellow blooms of its better-known relative Chrysothemis pulchella. Pinch stems periodically to keep growth compact and encourage repeat flowering.
